contributions.headingText: Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate is a malignant neoplasm thought to be derived from prostatic basal cells.
2C82.Y & XH4ZC3 Other specified malignant neoplasms of prostate & Basal cell carcinoma of the prostate
Acceptable: adenoid cystic carcinoma; adenoid basal cell carcinoma; basal cell carcinoma of the prostate; adenoid cystic carcinoma (solid pattern).

Patients often have urinary obstruction; diagnosis is most commonly made on transurethral resection specimens, less often on biopsy. Serum PSA is normal {14657711; 17460452; 21440997} unless there is a concomitant acinar carcinoma, which is found in a minority of cases {14657711; 17460452; 15371944; 25870120}.
A subset of cases are associated with MYB::NFIB fusion {31189999; 26089205}.

Most cases show varying proportions of (1) the adenoid cystic / cribriform pattern with inspissated secretions and (2) the basaloid pattern with small solid nests of basal cells. Less often, cords of cells or small tubules lined by a hyaline rim are seen. The stroma may be desmoplastic. Mitotic activity and Ki-67 proliferation index vary widely. Five criteria support the differential diagnosis from florid basal cell hyperplasia: cytoarchitectural atypia, invasive pattern into the stroma and between normal prostate acini, perineural invasion, necrosis (seen in a few cases), and extraprostatic extension.

Basal cell markers often label the outermost layer(s) of basal cell carcinoma, sparing the adluminal cells. Conversely, CK7 labels only adluminal cells {14657711}. PSA is expressed in a minority of cases. Labelling in neoplastic cells is negative to weak for AMACR and AR {30655983; 17460452; 25870120}. ERG is negative {25870120}. Strong BCL2 positivity and elevated Ki-67 have been proposed to have utility in the distinction of basal cell carcinoma from florid basal cell hyperplasia {9865831}. Like adenoid cystic carcinomas in other organs, 12 of 13 adenoid cystic carcinomas from the prostate were found to overexpress ERBB2 (HER2) strongly at the mRNA level, whereas acinar adenocarcinomas were negative {17142577}. ERBB2 protein expression was also positive, although some studies have shown contrary findings {25547910}.

Adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate should be distinguished from urothelial carcinoma, high-grade acinar adenocarcinoma, and neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC), as well as from metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma from a primary elsewhere (including the Cowper glands).

By FISH, 17–47% of adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinomas of the prostate harbour the MYB::NFIB fusion, a similar rate to that seen in their salivary gland counterparts {31189999; 26089205}. Most fusion-positive cases (57%) had adenoid cystic–like morphology, whereas 93% of fusion-negative cases did not have adenoid cystic–like features. The fusion is not found in benign basal cell proliferations {31189999}. TMPRSS2::ERG fusions have not been identified {25870120}.

Essential: basal cell morphology and immunophenotype; identification of malignant features (cytoarchitectural atypia, infiltration of non-neoplastic prostate, perineural invasion, necrosis); exclusion of metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma from a primary elsewhere, including the Cowper glands.
The eighth edition of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) TNM system is used for staging.

Extraprostatic extension of adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate at radical prostatectomy has been reported in 44–71% of cases {31189999; 17460452}. Distant metastasis occurred in 14–29% of patients, half of whom died from the disease {14657711; 17460452; 15371944}. Thus, adenoid cystic (basal cell) carcinoma of the prostate is a potentially aggressive neoplasm requiring ablative therapy.
